payload.set_intro: A clinician records the following information during an intake visit with a 34-year-old adult who sought help because of constant worry.

rows: Worries about money, health, and work almost every day
Repeated unwanted thoughts that are neutralized by rituals

items.stem: Which diagnostic category best fits the information in the intake record?

options.text: Generalized anxiety disorder, because the worry is excessive, long-lasting, and accompanied by tension and sleep problems
options.why: Persistent worry about many topics with physical symptoms and no panic attacks or rituals points to generalized anxiety.

options.text: Panic disorder, because the person experiences frequent physical symptoms
options.why: The record shows no sudden episodes of intense fear, which panic disorder requires.

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, because the person experiences repeated worry
options.why: The record shows no rituals performed to neutralize unwanted thoughts.

options.text: Specific phobia, because the worry is linked to health and work
options.why: The record shows no avoidance of specific places or objects, and the worry covers many topics.

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is Generalized anxiety disorder, because the worry is excessive, long-lasting, and accompanied by tension and sleep problems. Persistent worry about many topics with physical symptoms and no panic attacks or rituals points to generalized anxiety.
Panic disorder, because the person experiences frequent physical symptoms is incorrect: The record shows no sudden episodes of intense fear, which panic disorder requires.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder, because the person experiences repeated worry is incorrect: The record shows no rituals performed to neutralize unwanted thoughts.
Specific phobia, because the worry is linked to health and work is incorrect: The record shows no avoidance of specific places or objects, and the worry covers many topics.

options.text: Free association about early childhood memories

items.stem: A researcher wants to use this intake record as evidence about adults with excessive worry in general. Which limitation of the record is most important?

options.text: It includes too many symptoms for the clinician to make a diagnosis
options.why: Several related symptoms are what make a diagnosis possible.

options.text: It is based on reported symptoms, which makes the record worthless for any purpose
options.why: Reported symptoms are an ordinary part of clinical records and are useful for diagnosis.

options.text: It describes only one person, so the findings may not apply to adults in general
options.why: A single case cannot show what is typical of a larger population.

options.text: It has no control group, so it cannot describe this person's symptoms accurately
options.why: A control group is needed to test causes, not to describe one person's symptoms.

difficulty.rationale: The item asks students to match one treatment technique (progressive muscle relaxation) to the physical symptoms in a short intake table. The table's negatives rule out phobia, panic and OCD-type treatments. The distractors (systematic desensitization for specific fears, flooding for panic, free association) are clearly mismatched to the record. This takes one concept application, a quick table read, and no computation.

difficulty.label: basic_learning
difficulty.rationale: The item asks students to identify the key limitation of a single case record: it cannot be generalized to adults in general. This applies one named concept (case study limits on generalizability) to a short scenario. The table is small and the stimulus needs no real interpretation, since the question does not depend on identifying the disorder. The distractors are clearly wrong. One is an absolute claim ('worthless'), one confuses a control group with descriptive accuracy, and one wrongly says too many symptoms prevent diagnosis. There are no near-miss options, and the item takes only about two reasoning steps with no computation.
